deep.reconstruction:
This page is a working draft of passages that ended up, in revised form, in Riemann's Inaugural Dissertation (Göttingen 1851), 'Grundlagen für eine allgemeine Theorie der Functionen einer veränderlichen complexen Grösse'. The surrounding pages fit this: the previous page treats log(z−z'), and the next page ('II 6', §. 9) treats the boundary-normal coordinates (s,p) and the Gauss–Green theorem leading to the Cauchy integral theorem. There is no derivation on this page. It contains foundational stipulations, written in several crossed-out attempts.

(1) Restricting discontinuities to isolated lines and points. Riemann says the discontinuities of the functions considered must be confined to isolated lines and points. Otherwise the functions could not appear in integrals extended over the surface T. A later variant (A) adds that this restriction is not required by the concept of a function as such (i.e. Dirichlet's arbitrary correspondence). It is required only so that the infinitesimal calculus can be applied.

He gives an example of a function discontinuous at every point of the surface. The first version, crossed out: f(x,y) = (value) when x and y are both commensurable (rational). The revised version: f(x,y) = 1 for incommensurable (irrational) x together with commensurable (rational) y, and f(x,y) = 2 otherwise. He says such a function admits neither differentiation nor integration, hence no infinitesimal calculus at all. This is a two-variable analogue of Dirichlet's 1829 nowhere-continuous function.

Implicit reasoning (mine): both sets {x irrational, y rational} and its complement are dense in every open set. So every neighbourhood contains values 1 and 2, and f is continuous nowhere. On every rectangle the upper Darboux sum is 2·area and the lower sum is 1·area. So f is not integrable in the Cauchy/Riemann sense.

(2) He states that the restriction placed here on the surface T will be justified later (Art. 15).

(3) Removable discontinuities. In a fragment headed '5,' and in a fuller version, he excludes, for u and for v, discontinuities that can be removed by changing the value at isolated points. The final wording, matching the printed dissertation: by convention a function of z shall have no discontinuity removable by changing its value at a single point.

(4) Definition of a function of z, essentially the printed text. Consider w = u + v i which, generally speaking (exceptions on isolated lines and points not excluded), has for each point O of T a definite value. This value varies continuously with the position of O and in accordance with u_x = v_y, u_y = −v_x (Cauchy–Riemann). This property is what is meant by calling w a function of z = x + y i. Riemann's concept of an analytic function is thus defined by continuity plus the CR equations, not by power series.

(5) Topological hypothesis. The surface T is first assumed to be simply connected and spread simply (schlicht, without branch points or overlapping sheets) over the plane A. Then follows the heading 'Lehrsatz', whose theorem (the integral theorem) is developed on the next page.
errors: No mathematical errors. The claim that the everywhere-discontinuous function cannot be integrated is correct for the integral concepts of the time (Cauchy/Riemann). In the modern Lebesgue sense it is integrable: it equals 2 almost everywhere, so its integral is 2·area. 'Cannot be subjected to the infinitesimal calculus' is thus historically contingent.
The first attempt at the example is left incomplete ('den Werth' with no values) before being replaced by the 1/2 version.

results.what: Analytic function defined by continuity plus the Cauchy–Riemann equations u_x=v_y, u_y=-v_x on a surface T, with exceptions allowed on isolated lines and points
Two-variable everywhere-discontinuous function (1 if x irrational and y rational, else 2) used to show the necessity of restricting discontinuities for integration
Convention excluding removable discontinuities (values changed at single points)
results.modern_name: Removable singularity convention / identification of functions differing at isolated points

results.what: Assumption that T is simply connected and schlicht over the plane before stating the integral theorem
results.modern_name: Simply connected domain hypothesis for Cauchy's integral theorem

deep.surprise_reason: This is a draft of known passages of the 1851 dissertation. The two-variable Dirichlet-function example is a minor draft detail, possibly cut from the printed version, of mild interest for the history of the integrability concept leading to the 1854 Habilitationsschrift.

transcription_corrections: The example is split across columns. The left column breaks off at 'für ganz commensurable Werthe von x und y den Werth', and the right column carries the revised continuation 'durchaus [für commensurable struck] incommensurables x und ein commensurables y den Werth 1, sonst [andernfalls struck] aber den Werth 2 hat ...'.

In the right column, 'also überhaupt der Infinitesimalrechnung' has 'unmittelbar' struck in parentheses. The insertion above appears to read 'unmittelbar', with 'überhaupt' struck at the end of the line. The reading of which word survives is uncertain.
The final line likely reads '... einfache Ausbreitung über die Ebene A beigelegt' (reading plausible), followed by 'Lehrsatz.'
'5,' at the start of the right-column fragment is probably an article/section number, followed by a struck word (perhaps 'Die').
